question: A 50-year-old man comes to the physician because of gradually worsening rhythmic movements of his right hand for the past 5 months. His symptoms worsen when he is in a meeting and he is concerned that people are noticing it more frequently. There is no personal or family history of serious illness, but the patient recalls that his father developed bobbing of the head in older age. He takes no medications. Neurological examination shows a tremor of the right hand when the limbs are relaxed. When the patient is asked to move his arm the tremor decreases. He has reduced arm swing while walking. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Gradually worsening rhythmic movements of right hand" -> "Tremor of right hand at rest" -> "Reduced arm swing while walking" -> "Essential tremor" -> "First-line treatment is propranolol" -> 80%

enhanced_information: The patient presents with gradually worsening rhythmic movements of the right hand, tremor at rest, and reduced arm swing while walking, suggestive of essential tremor. The most appropriate pharmacotherapy for essential tremor is propranolol as first-line treatment, not trihexyphenidyl, clonazepam, or levodopa/carbidopa.
analysis: The patient's presentation with gradually worsening rhythmic movements of the right hand, tremor at rest, and reduced arm swing while walking is consistent with essential tremor. Propranolol is the first-line pharmacotherapy for essential tremor based on standard medical knowledge. Trihexyphenidyl, clonazepam, and levodopa/carbidopa are not the preferred treatments for essential tremor.
